name: Colin Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a company of about forty people that makes timetable software for schools: which teacher is in which room, with which class, at what time. I'm a junior on the testing side. I write the automatic tests that check a timetable doesn't put two classes in the science lab at once, and I look after the import that pulls pupil lists in from each school's own system, which breaks every September when the new year starts.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, all the time. I built a little bot over a weekend that reads a bug report and drafts the test cases for it, and now half the team uses it. To be fair, that's partly because I'm not great at writing tests from scratch yet. The bot covers for me, and I know it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like messing about with new tools and seeing if they actually help. What wears me out is money. I share a house with two others, and after rent and my college loan I've got about two weeks of money in the bank at any time. My mum works on the front desk at a primary school, funnily enough, and she uses our software, so I hear about it when it's broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool that got oversold. My test bot is still useful, it saves maybe an hour a day, but it doesn't think. I'd probably post a write-up on how I actually use it, the real numbers, not the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine but not great. Schools pay for our software every year, so the company's steady, but I'm still a junior on low pay with two weeks of money behind me. If anything I'd be a bit disappointed, because I was hoping the tools would carry me further than my own skills do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the bot and make it better, and use the time it saves to actually learn to write good tests myself. I'd ask our lead, Rashid, about moving up a grade by the end of next year. And I'd set up an automatic transfer of fifty a month into savings on payday, before I can spend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, and still uneasy about money. It's not an AI problem, it's a junior-pay problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you were hoping the tools would carry you further. What did you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I hoped I'd never have to get really good at the hard bits, because the AI would. If AI plateaus, I have to grind like everyone did before. That's fair, I suppose, but it's slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the hour a day the bot saves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Read other people's test code, properly, the way Rashid keeps telling me to. Maybe do one small course on testing. The bot buys me time; whether I use it well is on me.

say: AI is a **decent tool** that got oversold.
I'd post the **real numbers** on how my test bot saves about an hour a day.
think: The company is **steady** because schools pay every year, but my pay is low.
I hoped the tools would carry me further than **my own skills** do.
do: Use the hour the bot saves to **learn testing** properly.
Ask Rashid about moving **up a grade** by the end of next year.
Set up an automatic **fifty a month** into savings on payday.
feel: **A bit flat**, and still uneasy about money.
S0.quote: If AI plateaus, I have to grind like everyone did before.
fieldNote: Colin admits his bot **covers for weak skills**; a plateau forces him to grind.
His employer feels **steady**, since schools renew every year.
He frames his worry as **junior pay**, not AI.

steps.text: Improve the test-drafting bot the team already uses
Spend the bot's saved hour reading senior colleagues' test code
Move fifty a month into savings automatically on payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get on board, and I'd be the one at work running sessions on how to use it. Online I'd say the same: learn it or get left. Not in a nasty way, just practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a better spot than most juniors, because I've already built the thing the company will want more of. Checking and coding are both on the list, so the team will shrink, but someone has to set up and look after the AI testing, and right now that's me. The risk is a senior who's better than me picks it up and doesn't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Rashid in the first month and pitch turning my bot into a proper tool for the whole team, with me in charge of it. I'd take a short course on how AI testing tools are built, maybe two hundred, paid by the company if I can swing it. And I'd keep saving the fifty a month, more if I get a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a bit of worry. For the first time, being a junior who likes new tools is an advantage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the team would shrink. Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah and Joe, the two manual testers who click through every screen before a release. They're careful and good, but that clicking is exactly what the tools take over. I'd feel bad that my bot is part of why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company decides it doesn't need a junior to run the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have something good on my CV, at least, and I'd look for remote jobs. There's only a couple of software firms near me, so remote is the real option. It would be tight with two weeks of savings, I won't pretend otherwise.

say: This is the moment to **get on board** with AI.
I'd run **sessions at work** showing people how to use it.
think: I've already built the **AI testing** tool the company will want more of.
The risk is a **better senior** picking it up and not needing me.
do: Pitch Rashid on turning my bot into a **team tool** I run.
Take a **short course** on AI testing tools, ideally company-paid.
Keep saving **fifty a month**, more after any raise.
feel: **Mostly excited**, with some worry, because liking new tools is finally an advantage.
S1.quote: For the first time, being a junior who likes new tools is an advantage.
fieldNote: Colin is **well placed** and knows it, but sees a senior as the threat.
He feels **guilty** that his bot helps replace two manual testers.
With **two weeks** of savings, remote jobs are his only fallback.

steps.text: Pitch Rashid on turning the test bot into a team tool
Take a short course on AI testing tools, ideally company-paid
Keep saving fifty a month and raise it after any pay rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and we need proper support for people, fast, because two years is nothing. I'm not usually a politics person, but this would need governments acting quickly. I'd say that online and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my head start with the tools buys me a year at most. If AI can do almost any thinking work by 2028, it doesn't need a junior to set it up. All my work is screen work, so the robots coming later in 2031 don't protect me at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd make as much money as I can from being the AI guy, maybe freelancing in the evenings setting up AI tools for small firms, because everyone would be scrambling. I'd save everything I make on the side. And I'd look at what's hands-on and lasts until 2031; my uncle fits kitchens, and I'm handy enough, so I'd ask him about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. Under the excitement I'd be properly scared, because I'm good at riding the wave, not at surviving after it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Freelancing on the side while the wave hits. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything's risky in that picture. For about a year, firms would pay for someone to set up AI tools for them, and I can do that. After that the tools set themselves up. So it's a year of making hay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum her job on the school front desk might actually outlast mine, because parents like a face. Then I'd tell her not to worry, which she'd ignore. She worries about me more than about herself.

say: Two years is **nothing**, so people need **proper support** fast.
Governments would have to **act quickly**, and I'd say that online.
think: My **head start** with the tools buys me a year at most.
All my work is **screen work**, so robots in 2031 don't protect me.
do: **Freelance** evenings setting up AI tools for small firms, for about a year.
Ask my uncle about **fitting kitchens** for the hands-on years until 2031.
feel: **Alarmed** under the excitement: good at riding waves, not at **surviving after**.
S2.quote: I'm good at riding the wave, not at surviving after it.
fieldNote: Colin turns his skill into a **one-year cash window** through freelancing.
He sees the **robot gap** as a shelter only through his uncle's kitchen-fitting work.
His mum's **front-desk job** might outlast his, which he says gently.

steps.text: Freelance evenings setting up AI tools for small local firms
Save all freelance earnings in a separate account
Ask his uncle about a kitchen-fitting job before 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, if we're honest about it now. Companies should be retraining staff instead of waiting. I'd say that at work, and I'd push for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means a few good years. I'd be the AI person at work, maybe get promoted by 2028, and earn a bit more. Then 2031 ends the screen work, and I'd need something else by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead the AI testing at work and push for a mid-level title within two years. I'd start the freelancing now, setting up tools for small firms, and grow it slowly. And I'd use the money to train in something practical; I'd probably take an electrician's course from about 2029, because robots for that only arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious, which suits me. I'd rather be running than sitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an electrician's course rather than kitchens with your uncle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Electricians earn more, and every house that gets fancy new robots and chargers will need rewiring. My uncle says that himself. Kitchens would be the backup if the course is full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut while you're doing all that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nights out, mostly. And I'd probably move into a cheaper room, there's one going in my friend Dev's house for eighty less a month. Five years of eighty is a course paid for.

say: Five years is **short but workable** if we're honest now.
Companies should be **retraining staff** instead of waiting.
think: A few good years as the **AI person**, maybe promoted by 2028.
In **2031** the screen work ends and I'd need something else.
do: Lead the **AI testing** and push for a mid-level title within two years.
Start **freelancing** now, setting up tools for small firms.
feel: **Busy-anxious**, which suits him: he'd rather be running than sitting.
S3.quote: Every house that gets fancy new robots and chargers will need rewiring.
fieldNote: Colin plans **three tracks** at once: AI lead, freelancing, then a trade.
He picks **electrical work** because robots need wiring, an inventive reason.
A **cheaper room** would pay for the course.

steps.text: Lead the school-timetable team's AI testing and seek a mid-level title
Set up AI tools for small local firms on evenings
Move into the cheaper room in Dev's house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't use it is choosing not to. Learn the tools, build skills, have a plan. Probably a bit smug, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think this is the best one for me. Ten years of being the person who's good with AI is a whole career. I'd be thirty-seven, probably mid-level or senior, with savings, and I'd pick my next move from a strong place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow into a proper role around AI testing over the next three years and push for real pay rises. I'd save steadily, aiming for three months by 2029. I'd keep an eye on the trades but wouldn't start anything until about 2032, when I can see what's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. The money's still tight now, and it's still on my mind, but there's room to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sound a bit smug. Is that fair to people in different jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, probably not. My mum couldn't just learn new tools at her age with her hours. I should say it's plenty for people like me, not for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change in your personal life with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop sharing a house eventually, maybe get a place with my girlfriend, if I have one by then. With two years I'd stay put to save money. With ten I'd let myself plan a normal life.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, and anyone who doesn't use it is choosing not to.
Learn the tools, **build skills** and have a plan.
think: Ten years of being **good with AI** is a whole career.
At **thirty-seven** I'd pick my next move from a strong place.
do: Grow into a proper **AI testing role** over three years.
Wait until about **2032** before starting anything in the trades.
feel: **Uneasy but mostly fine**, because money is tight but there's room to fix it.
S4.quote: Ten years of being the person who's good with AI is a whole career.
fieldNote: Colin catches his own **smugness** and corrects it when asked about his mum.
With ten years he allows himself **normal life plans**.
His remaining worry is today's **low pay**, not AGI.

steps.text: Build a full AI testing role at the timetable company
Save three months of expenses by 2029
Hold off on any trade course until about 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My one advantage, being good with the tools, would last about a year. What would help is cheap, fast training in hands-on trades, and some income support so I could take it without losing my room.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to help build the thing. My test bot is a tiny version of what replaces Hannah and Joe. I'm proud of my test bot and a bit ashamed of it at the same time.

headlineQuote: I'm proud of my test bot and a bit ashamed of it at the same time.
portrait: Colin, 27, writes **automatic tests** for a company that makes timetable software for schools.
He uses AI **every day** and built a test-drafting bot the team relies on, partly to cover weak skills.
He shares a house, pays off a college loan and has about **two weeks** of savings.
He feels **well placed** in slower change, but sees his edge lasting only a year in AGI by 2028.
His fallbacks are **freelancing** setting up AI tools and then electrical work before robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his one advantage with the tools would last about a year.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, fast **trade training** plus income support so he could keep his room.
